source_title: The 25 best horror movies based on true stories - Entertainment Weekly
source_excerpt:
Courtesy Everett Collection (2); Michael Tackett/New Line / Warner Bros
Horror thrives in abstract spaces — the unknown, the unreal, the inexplicable, the irrational. It takes advantage of the darkness within our imagination. And yet sometimes the best way to tap into our deep-seated fears is simply to read an old newspaper clipping. Perhaps the ghastly cinematic monster wearing someone’s skin for a face was, in reality, just some guy from Wisconsin.
The scariest thing in a horror movie isn’t always the house-haunting spirit, knife-wielding madman, or bloodthirsty monster — sometimes, it’s these five words: “Based on a true story.” Of course, as our culture’s obsession with true crime has proven, we love being scared by real-life nightmares even more than those conjured by creepy clowns or demon-possessed dolls.
It may be uncomfortable to realize how many horror movies have turned real events into cinematic nightmares, but it’s true. From demons to death cults, uncaught killers to unsolved disappearances, these genre films have proven that truth is not just stranger, but also scarier than fiction.
With that in mind, turn off the lights, turn on your favorite streaming device, and brace yourself for Entertainment Weekly ’s list of the 25 best horror movies inspired by true stories.
First Look Pictures/courtesy Everett Collection
The torture and murder of 16-year-old Sylvia Likens — who was subjected to unspeakable abuse by her guardian Gertrude Baniszewski, the woman’s daughter Paula and son John, and other neighborhood kids — inspired the 2007 film An American Crime .
Likens was beaten, kicked, thrown down stairs, branded, and had cigarettes put out on her skin. By the time it was over, she was “malnourished and covered with sores, burns, and bruises,” according to The Indianapolis Star . She died on Oct. 26, 1965. Baniszewski was convicted of first-degree murder in 1966.
One of the darkest true stories on this list, An American Crime never undersells or soft-pedals the ceaseless agony of Likens’ ordeal. Elliot Page conveys the young teen’s vitality and promise, while a blood-freezing Catherine Keener is the sinister embodiment of resentment and cruelty. On paper, the story sounds like the thinking man’s torture porn — and yet the inexplicable real-life details confirm that much of the film’s horror is rooted in fact.
Where to watch An American Crime : Prime Video
American International/Courtesy Everett
On Nov. 13, 1974, Ronald DeFeo Jr. shot and killed six members of his family in Amityville, N.Y. A year later, George and Kathy Lutz moved into the same house with their three children, only to flee within a month after reportedly experiencing an onslaught of paranormal activity, including mysterious voices and green slime oozing from the walls.
The Lutzes’ claims have been contested since the publication of Jay Anson’s 1977 book. Famed paranormal investigators Ed and Lorraine Warren concluded that there was a genuine supernatural presence within the home. However, DeFeo’s lawyer claimed that he and the Lutzes “created this horror story over many bottles of wine… We were really playing with each other. We were creating something the public would want to hear about.”
Call it an enduring supernatural phenomenon or really good salesmanship, but everyone knows about The Amityville Horror , whether they’ve seen it on screen or not. The widely publicized murders and alleged hauntings associated with the house spawned an entire franchise of mediocre movies that stray further from the original story with each entry.
The original 1979 shocker helped cement the tropes of haunted-house pictures that endure to this day. Margot Kidder and James Brolin star as the Lutzes in a highly fictionalized version of this already embellished “true” story. The slayings are depicted at the start of the movie and underpin the Lutzes’ subsequent visions. The pacing is quintessentially ’70s, which is to say deliberate, yet the film works all the better for it, rooting the horror in suspense and a vintage visual sheen.
Where to watch The Amityville Horror : AMC+
In 1961, the peaceful Monterey Bay community of Capitola, Calif., was shaken by the sudden, bizarre behavior of seabirds. Unlike the movie’s winged menaces, the birds weren’t pecking the eyes out of unsuspecting townsfolk, but they were acting violently and erratically — not just slamming into homes, power lines, and lampposts, but delivering the occasional bite as well.
When all was said and done, “hundreds” of birds were “laying all over the streets,” as one local recalled. Decades later, the phenomenon was studied, and scientists linked the behavior to a neurotoxin produced by algae that entered the birds’ food supply.
Alfred Hitchcock ’s beak-bearing classic is based on British author Daphne du Maurier’s short story about flocks of violent birds that suddenly attack a small farm and its surrounding community in Cornwall, England. The sudden and inexplicable bird attacks take on a genuinely apocalyptic flavor when all is said and done.
In 2004, an 18-year-old girl working at a Kentucky McDonald’s was “ detained, stripped, and sexually assaulted ” at the instruction of an anonymous caller claiming to be a policeman. According to prosecutors, the phone call lasted hours and the victim was forced into sex acts with the restaurant assistant manager’s fiancé.
The accused, 38-year-old Florida resident David Stewart, was acquitted at his 2006 trial but remained a suspect in a series of similar phone call hoaxes dating back to 1994. McDonald’s was ordered to pay $6.1 million in damages, but appealed the ruling and later settled out of court.
Craig Zobel’s film is anchored in realism, remaining largely faithful to the details of the real case without veering into exploitation territory. Dreama Walker plays Becky, the young fast-food worker victimized by the phone creep (Pat Healy) when he accuses her of stealing from a customer. Sandra (Ann Dowd), the manager, obeys the caller’s increasingly perverse requests and becomes startlingly devoted to the task while the other employees begin to sense something is off.
Compliance is a queasy thriller, a hostage drama that renders the universal fear of captivity in such visceral fashion that it will leave you dripping in cold sweat.
Where to watch Compliance : Prime Video (to rent)
Michael Tackett/New Line/Warner Bros
Perhaps the world’s most famous paranormal investigators, Ed and Lorraine Warren spent decades investigating reports of ghostly phenomena. The Conjuring was inspired by the Perron family’s alleged haunting at their Rhode Island farmhouse, which, contrary to the film’s compressed timeline, spanned their residency from 1971 to 1980.
The Warrens came to believe that the property was haunted by the spirit of a woman named Bathsheba Sherman, whom they believed was a witch who had cursed the land, ensuring that anyone who lived there would meet a grisly demise. Andrea Perron, the eldest child, told USA Today that The Conjuring was “a beautiful tapestry” that contains “many elements of truth to it, and some moments of fiction.”
This may go down as James Wan ’s seminal work. It combines three elements at which the filmmaker excels: creeping, gnawing dread; space for his talented cast to create real characters and stakes; and an over-the-top freakout final act that winks knowingly at the audience without betraying the horror of the premise.
After making an ill-fated move into the farmhouse, the Perrons (led by Lili Taylor as the mother, Carolyn) deal with supernatural visions, sounds, smells, and direct encounters before eventually bringing Ed and Lorraine to the property. Vera Farmiga and Patrick Wilson portray the Warrens in a film that spawned not only several direct sequels but an entire shared universe.
Where to watch The Conjuring : HBO Max
After the success of The Fly (1986), David Cronenberg returned to a long-gestating project inspired by the strange tale of Stewart and Cyril Marcus. The identical-twin gynecologists , who practiced on the Upper East Side, were found dead in Cyril’s apartment a few blocks from their practice. The unit was caked in grime that had accumulated over a significant amount of time, though what killed them was not immediately clear. Some speculated it was a suicide pact or perhaps a case of folie à deux.
There remain competing theories over their causes of death. Investigators initially theorized that both died of barbiturate withdrawal, but subsequent findings complicated that conclusion. Ultimately, the medical examiner determined that Stewart died of a barbiturate overdose , while Cyril’s cause of death remains uncertain.
Cronenberg’s demented dark comedy about the social machinations of identical-twin gynecologists (both played by Jeremy Irons) combines the icky body horror and frank sexual politics of the director’s early work with the more high-minded dramatics of his later career.
Along with Irons, Geneviève Bujold gives one of her most nuanced performances as the woman caught between the brothers’ manipulations. Dead Ringers is one of Cronenberg’s most vibrantly inspired pictures, one that has you glued to the screen even as you wish to squirm away.
Where to watch Dead Ringers : Prime Video (to rent)
Ed Gein , the odd-jobber known as “The Butcher of Plainfield,” had a habit of robbing graves, exhuming the corpses, and using pieces of their bones and skin to adorn his home. In November 1957, after the disappearance of hardware store owner Bernice Worden, he was arrested on suspicion of her murder. Police discovered Worden’s savagely mutilated corpse strung upside down in Gein’s shed.
Gein admitted to robbing the graves of middle-aged women who resembled his mother, having begun the habit after her death in 1945. Gein was found guilty of first-degree murder in 1968, but in a separate phase of the proceedings, he was found legally insane at the time of the killing.
There are a couple of much more famous horror movies that claim inspiration (loose as it may be) from Gein. In fact, they’re even on this list. But while The Texas Chain Saw Massacre and Psycho merely plucked specific details and otherwise invented the rest, Deranged sticks much closer to the real-life story.
Framed as something of a faux-documentary, the film features a reporter addressing the audience to explain that the events really took place — and that only names and locations have been changed. From there, we witness the life and grave-robbing times of Ezra Cobb, a Gein-like weirdo who spent a lifetime doting on his domineering mother hand and foot… and keeps right on doing so after she dies. Eventually he adds a few guests.
Largely overlooked upon its initial release, the movie developed a cult following after resurfacing on VHS in the ‘90s, despite its sensationalist subtitle, Confessions of a Necrophile .
20th Century Fox /Courtesy Everett Collection
The Entity was inspired by the case of Doris Bither. In 1974, the California woman claimed that she and her children were victims of a sinister haunting and that paranormal entities subjected her to repeated physical and sexual assaults. Eventually, two parapsychologists, Barry Taff and Kerry Gaynor, were brought in to investigate .
One of the more bizarre supernatural films inspired by a true story, The Entity spins the tale of Carla Moran (Barbara Hershey), a single mother who’s physically and sexually abused by an unseen force terrorizing her Los Angeles home.
On the surface, the film’s premise might seem like a uniquely diabolical take on the popular possession and haunted-house tropes of the era. But its relationship to the Bither case only makes it stranger and more unnerving.
Where to watch The Entity : Prime Video
In 1960s Germany, teenager Anneliese Michel began to suffer mysterious blackout episodes. She was diagnosed with epilepsy and prescribed medication, but her health declined further. She claimed to see the devil and hear demons cursing her as she prayed. After years of attempts to rid her body of this presumed evil, authorization to perform an exorcism was granted.
Over 10 months, priests Ernst Alt and Arnold Renz performed 67 exorcisms on Michel. During the sessions, she suffered severe injuries to her knees, including damaged ligaments, from repeatedly kneeling in prayer. On July 1, 1976, she died at age 23, weighing 68 pounds . The cause of death was malnutrition and dehydration. Alt, Renz, and Michel’s parents were later convicted of negligent homicide.
Scott Derrickson directed this unexpectedly moving horror procedural , which is loosely inspired by the Michel case while updating the story for the multiplex crowd. Laura Linney is especially good as the agnostic lawyer representing the priest (Tom Wilkinson) who oversaw the fatal exorcism; however, it’s Jennifer Carpenter who carries the film as the eponymous Emily. She delivers a frenzied, frightened performance that never loses sight of the real-life tragedy.
Even amid the film’s focus on sleuthing and courtroom drama, the unsettling possession scenes — shown as flashbacks during the trial — are some of the scariest committed to film.
Where to watch The Exorcism of Emily Rose : Prime Video (to rent)
In writing his original novel, William Peter Blatty researched a 1949 case in which priests performed 20 to 30 exorcisms on a 13-year-old boy to purportedly rid the child of demonic possession. During all but the final exorcism, the child reportedly thrashed about while shouting profanities and phrases in Latin, a language he had never studied. During the final session, there were no utterances from the boy, and afterward, no further disturbances were reported.
The Maryland teenager was long known as “Roland Doe.” He went on to live a long life and work as an engineer at NASA. After his death in 2020, his actual identity was publicly revealed as Ronald Edwin Hunkeler .
Thanks to William Friedkin’s classic, possession and exorcism are key components of the pop-culture imagination. But he saw the film as a more somber exercise.
“I did this film because I believe in the story. This film was made by a believer ,” Friedkin said in 2012 . “I know it’s voted this-and-that horror film, but to me, it’s about the mystery of faith.”
The fictionalized story unfolds in the then-present day, with the boy reimagined as Regan (Linda Blair), the adolescent daughter of a movie star. But Friedkin’s declared commitment to the enigma of faith in the face of supernatural events — embodied, in different ways, by the priests played by Max von Sydow and Jason Miller — distinguishes it from the many possession films that came before and after it.
Where to watch The Exorcist : HBO Max
Paramount/courtesy Everett Collection
Set in 1975, Fire in the Sky is loosely adapted from Travis Walton’s book The Walton Experience , which details his claims of having been kidnapped by extraterrestrials. Walton, who was working as a logger in northeastern Arizona, disappeared for five days after he and his coworkers reported spotting a strange, illuminated object in the sky. While the rest of his logging crew returned home, Walton claimed to have spent part of his disappearance aboard an alien spacecraft.
This alien-abduction tale leans more towards sci-fi, with a memorable detour into otherworldly body horror. D.B. Sweeney plays Walton, and the story beats more or less follow the broad outlines of his account. The logging crew sees a strange light in the sky, Walton disappears, and the others are initially suspected of having a hand in his disappearance. Until, that is, their buddy reappears with vague recollections of having been abducted and experimented upon inside an alien spacecraft.
With Walton’s recollections as fragmented as they were, the filmmakers took liberties with the abduction sequences. As Walton himself put it : “ Fire in the Sky is not a documentary. I’m sure audiences will feel what I felt during the abduction… like a lab specimen.”
Where to watch Fire in the Sky : Prime Video (to rent)
This low-budget deep cut is based on an especially macabre case from 1828 that has gone down in legend in the U.K. Irish-born serial killers William Burke and William Hare killed at least 16 people for… well, let’s call it a stroke of entrepreneurial spirit. A local anatomist and private lecturer, Dr. Robert Knox, needed fresh cadavers for research, dissection, and medical demonstrations — and paid for them.
Just like that, the duo had stumbled upon an unexpected business opportunity. After initially selling the body of a lodger who had died of natural causes, they quickly moved to outright murder.
George Rose and Donald Pleasence play Burke and Hare in The Flesh and the Fiends , with horror legend Peter Cushing as Dr. Knox. Decades later, none other than Simon Pegg and Andy Serkis played the homicidal duo in John Landis’ Burke and Hare (2010), with Tom Wilkinson as the infamous surgeon.
Where to watch The Flesh and the Fiends : Prime Video (to rent)
Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer (1986)
Greycat Films/courtesy Everett Collection
Long before our culture’s true-crime obsession turned an entire generation into Netflix-addicted armchair detectives, this gritty, low-budget sorta-true story stirred up plenty of controversy. Featuring Michael Rooker in his chilling debut, Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer is loosely based on real-life killer Henry Lee Lucas and his friend (and occasional murderous sidekick) Ottis Toole.
The real Henry, it turns out, was a rather extreme fabulist — a killer, yes, but without nearly the body count he claimed. He said he killed hundreds of people, but most of those confessions turned out to be false.
Rooker’s take on the character is soft-spoken, and his violence is downright casual. That matter-of-factness is what gives the film its unsettling pull. It’s the movie’s sense of grim authenticity, as much as its violence, that earned it an X rating. Following several years of festival screenings and distribution delays, an unrated version of the divisive movie was finally released in 1990.
Where to watch Henry: Portrait of a Serial Killer : Prime Video
Universal Pictures/Courtesy of Getty
Everyone knows Jaws the movie. And most are also aware it was based on Peter Benchley’s 1974 novel.
What’s not as well known is that the author was partly inspired by a 1964 newspaper story about a massive great white shark caught off Long Island. The novel also bears striking parallels to a series of very real shark attacks that took place in 1916 along the Jersey Shore. Legs were bitten off, an 11-year-old boy was among the fatalities, and just like the movie, a bounty was eventually put on the man-eating shark’s head. President Woodrow Wilson even convened a Cabinet meeting about it. Eventually, a shark hunter with a much less cool name than Quint caught a shark and beat it to death with a broken oar handle. Human bones were reportedly found inside.
Jaws is widely recognized as Steven Spielberg’s big breakthrough, the first summer blockbuster, and the best reason to never go back to the beach. Quint, Hooper, Brody, and of course Bruce (the mechanical shark) have gone down in history — but the movie also had an impact on real-life sharks. It was “ a turning point for great white sharks ” in terms of public perception and helped fuel a wave of shark trophy hunting. For his part, Spielberg says he “truly regret[s]” the unintended repercussions.
In trouble with the law since she was 18, serial killer Aileen Wuornos went on a killing spree between 1989 and 1990. While working as a prostitute, she shot and killed at least six men in just under 12 months and confessed to a seventh murder. She was ultimately caught, convicted, and executed for her crimes.
Monster received as much attention for Charlize Theron’s dramatic physical transformation and acclaimed performance as it did for the chilling true story it adapted. The actress’ metamorphosis from classically beautiful leading lady to Aileen Wuornos was indeed something to behold. Theron won an Oscar for her lead performance, among a string of other awards.
The film holds largely true to her homicidal spree, while omitting various details about her life as well as combining or even inventing characters for dramatic purposes.
Where to watch Monster : Prime Video (to rent)
On Jan. 25, 1998, during a scuba diving trip in the Coral Sea, American couple Tom and Eileen Lonergan were abandoned in the ocean when their boat’s crew miscounted the passengers. It wasn’t until two days later, when the Lonergans’ personal items were discovered onboard, that anyone realized something was amiss. An intensive search was launched, but the pair were never found.
In the months that followed, some of the couple’s scuba gear washed ashore approximately 75 miles from where they had last been seen. A diver’s slate was also recovered at sea , bearing a desperate message dated Jan. 26, 1998: “Monday Jan 26; 1998 08am. To anyone who can help us: We have been abandoned on A[gin]court Reef by MV Outer Edge 25 Jan 1998 3pm. Please help to rescue us before we die. Help!!!”
If you ever wondered how it might feel to be stranded in a difficult relationship, then left in shark-infested waters with that person, Open Water is your answer. This somber fictionalization of the Lonergans’ ordeal sticks the audience squarely within the couple’s unenviable experience.
The filmmakers were so committed to achieving that sense of verisimilitude that they used real sharks alongside the actors . But it was director Chris Kentis, ostensibly protected in his baited cage, who had the most intense underwater encounter while trying to get the perfect close-up: “The shark barreled right into the cage, which was kind of like being stuck in a small elevator with a big shark.”
Serial killer Ed Gein (and his relationship with his mother) certainly left a mark on cinema. You won’t find a creepy motel in the true story, but Norman Bates’ psychological baggage bears eerie parallels to Gein’s dysfunctional upbringing. Like Gein, Bates (Anthony Perkins) was raised in relative isolation by a domineering mother who instilled in him an unhealthy, demeaning view of women.
Alfred Hitchcock’s genre-defining Psycho isn’t directly based on the real-life Wisconsin killer, but rather on Robert Bloch’s eponymous book, which drew inspiration from the circumstances surrounding Gein’s crimes. The novelist, who lived just 50 miles from the murderer, began writing the book the year after Gein was arrested.
The film pivots on the arrival of antiheroine Marion Crane (Janet Leigh) at the Bates Motel en route to a hoped-for new life after she embezzled $40,000 in cash. She and the manager, Norman, have a friendly chat — too friendly, as far as Norman’s mother is concerned, or so it seems when a figure resembling her proceeds to knife poor Marion to death. There is, of course, more to the story than that, and certainly more to Norman and the bag of bones in that basement chair.
The recording says it all: “I don’t care how many screams you hear, I don’t care how many anguished cries… Death is a million times preferable to 10 more days of this life.” That was the voice of Jim Jones, founder of the Peoples Temple, as the infamous 1978 mass murder-suicide at Jonestown unfolded.
The inciting incident of the cult’s demise was a California congressman traveling to Guyana with journalists and relatives of Peoples Temple members to investigate allegations of abuse at Jonestown. On Nov. 18, gunmen from the Peoples Temple attacked the congressman’s delegation as its members prepared to leave, killing the congressman, three journalists, and one defector. Jones subsequently ordered the deaths of more than 900 people at Jonestown, including hundreds of children.
